items.title: The abstract reads as machine-written, though its claims are sound
items.context: The whole abstract: the cost problem, the sampling idea, the main rate, the role of imbalance, and the simulations.
items.note: It reads as machine-written: fundamentally bottlenecked, offers a computational workaround, In this work we frame, Our primary contribution is, By utilizing, Furthermore, and three rendering-X participles in one sentence. The claims themselves are sound, and the patch keeps every one.
items.verified: yes -- every claim in the replacement checked against the body: the rate, the fixed-imbalance condition, the square-root-m saving, the two mechanisms and the cubic dependence all survive unchanged
items.coverage: the whole abstract body is replaced; the checker scored it 12.5 percent, the highest density in the document, yet flagged only one of its sentences

hunks.before:
Top-down reconstruction of latent binary phylogenetic trees is fundamentally bottlenecked by the $\Theta(m^2)$ cost of computing pairwise similarities across $m$ leaves. While observing only a sparse, Bernoulli-sampled subset of entries offers a computational workaround, real-world tree imbalance severely degrades the spectral signal, rendering standard balanced-cluster recovery guarantees inadequate. 
In this work, we frame spectral tree inference as an eigenvector perturbation problem within the matrix-completion regime, showing that the split obtained from the full similarity matrix of an imbalanced latent tree is recovered exactly from the sign pattern of the empirical Fiedler vector computed on a sparse sample. That split is an edge cut of the tree for any topology.

Our primary contribution is a sharp finite-sample guarantee proving that a sampling rate of $p = \Theta(\log m / m)$ suffices for exact recovery of that split at a fixed imbalance. By utilizing a coordinate-wise Neumann-series expansion rather than a standard Davis-Kahan $\ell_2$ transfer, we eliminate a spurious $\sqrt{m}$ factor in the entry-wise error bound. 
Furthermore, we identify the imbalance ratio $\eta$ as the governing topological parameter and prove it dictates recovery through two distinct failure mechanisms: artificially inflating subspace coherence (rendering recovery statistically unaffordable) and eroding the spectral gap (rendering recovery structurally impossible). 
This yields an explicit sample complexity dependence of $(1+\eta)^3$. Simulations on closed-form block models and Kingman coalescent trees with JC69 sequence evolution validate the predicted $\Theta(\log m / m)$ scaling and the isolated degradation mechanics of topological imbalance.
hunks.after:
Top-down spectral reconstruction of a latent binary phylogeny spends $\Theta(m^2)$ on pairwise similarities at its first split, before the recursion has taken a step. Sampling a Bernoulli subset of the entries removes that cost, but phylogenies are imbalanced, and the guarantees available for recursive spectral bipartitioning are stated for clusters of comparable size.
We treat recovery from a sample as an eigenvector perturbation problem. The split of the full similarity matrix is recovered exactly from the sign pattern of the Fiedler vector of a sparse sample, and that split is an edge cut of the tree for any topology.

A sampling rate $p=\Theta(\log m/m)$ suffices at fixed imbalance. Working coordinate-wise, through a Neumann expansion and a per-node Bernstein bound rather than a Davis-Kahan $\ell_2$ transfer, removes a $\sqrt m$ factor from the entry-wise error bound.
The imbalance ratio $\eta$ governs the result and enters twice: it raises the coherence of the leading subspace, which raises the sampling rate recovery needs, and it shrinks the spectral gap, which can close recovery off entirely. The rate depends on $\eta$ as $(1+\eta)^3$.
Simulations on closed-form block models and on Kingman trees with JC69 sequences reproduce the predicted $\Theta(\log m/m)$ scaling and separate the two mechanisms.

items.title: Two numbered results in the scaling section are never used
items.label: cor:infeasible
items.context: Two results in the scaling section. One says the guarantee becomes empty once the tree is too lopsided; the other defines coherence, a measure of how spread out the Fiedler vector is across the leaves.
items.note: Nothing uses either one. No later result builds on them and no sentence mentions them. Either they carry weight the paper never picks up, or they can go.
items.verified: yes -- deps.py reports zero dependants and zero prose sites; grep finds no \Cref to either label
items.statement:
\begin{corollary}[Vacuity of the certificate under imbalance]\label{cor:infeasible}
Under the hypotheses of \Cref{thm:main-sim}, with $\bze$ and the margin
$\rho-\eta\bze$ held bounded away from $0$ independently of $\eta$, the
right-hand side of \eqref{eq:main_rate} exceeds $1$ once
$\eta=\Omega\!\bigl(\sqrt[3]{m/\log m}\bigr)$; in general the threshold is
reached when $\eta^3\bze^2/(\rho-\eta\bze)^2=\Omega(m/\log m)$. No admissible sampling rate
$p\in(0,1]$ then satisfies the sufficient condition, so \Cref{thm:main-sim}
certifies nothing in that regime. What the theorem stops certifying there is the
sampling: \Cref{thm:stdr-split} continues to make $\Pisp{S}$ a split of
$\mathcal{T}$ whatever $\eta$ does.
\end{corollary}

items.title: A corollary about how lopsided the tree may be is proved, then never used
items.label: cor:tolerance
items.context: A corollary that turns the imbalance condition into a statement about the tree's shape: how uneven the tree is allowed to be, measured by its depth and its overall spread.
items.note: It has a proof in Appendix A, and after that nothing refers to it. No later result uses it and no sentence points at it. If it is meant to tell the reader when the method applies, the paper never says that; if not, it can go.
items.verified: yes -- deps.py finds the proof title and no other reference; grep returns exactly those two lines
items.statement:
\begin{corollary}[Structural imbalance tolerance]\label{cor:tolerance}
Measure the tree in log-similarity units: by \eqref{eq:similarity_gtr},
$r(\mathcal T):=\max_{i,j}(-\log S_{ij})=|\mathrm{tr}(Q)|\max_{i,j}d_{ij}$ is its diameter,
and $h(\mathcal T)$ its depth in the same units \cite{aizenbud2023spectral}, with
$h(\mathcal T)<r(\mathcal T)$.
Then a positive spectral gap is possible only if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:eta_distance_bound}
   \eta\le\mathcal O\!\bigl(e^{\mathcal O(h(\mathcal T))-r(\mathcal T)}\bigr).
\end{equation}
In particular, for an average Kingman coalescent tree, where
$r(\mathcal T),h(\mathcal T)=\mathcal O(\log m)$
\cite{erdos1999logs, aldous2001stochastic}, this gives $\eta\le\mathcal O(m^c)$ for
a model-dependent constant $c$.
\end{corollary}
